title: Wayseeking Mind
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart shares their personal journey from struggling with trauma and identity to finding peace and understanding through Zen practice. They reflect on how regular zazen practice helped them let go of goal-driven thinking and embrace a more present and spontaneous approach to life, allowing them to appreciate the beauty of uncertainty and interconnectedness. This shift in mindset has led to significant changes in their life and work, including applying Zen principles to their job as a code enforcement officer. Kanho invites the audience to consider this talk as a heartfelt but tentative expression, acknowledging that it is not a linear record of their practice or life.

Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Good morning, everybody.
Good morning.
How are you?
I'm doing great.
How's the [unclear: "shing"] going?
Good?
Thank you all very much for being here.
Without you it would be really boring if I just had to talk to myself up here.
I would like to say some things up front.
First, I want to thank Tim for inviting me to be Shuso and thereby allowing me to give this talk.
Tim has been there for all the years of my active practice and has put up with me patiently most of the time.
I thank my teacher, Norman Fischer, for accepting me as a student, for his support and encouragement and his teachings about gratitude and humility.
Arlene Luke supported me, and when I left Green Gulch she told me that regarding the two months there, there were three things I needed to remember.
One, there are no rules.
Two, it's not personal.
And three, have a big heart.
Luminous Owl Kokyo Henkel in Santa Cruz patiently helped and walked me through many, many services, with his friendly way of teaching.
Gratitude to teachers at Green Gulch and Tassajara and all the teachers I had the great fortune to encounter.
And thank you to you for being here.
Thank you for coming to this way seeking mind talk.
Or should I call it mind seeking way talk?
That almost seems to be more accurate to me, considering how my mind is behaving most of the time.
I've been thinking a bit about what a way seeking mind talk might be, and I realize there is no way I could do this phrase justice.
Decades of subtle influences seem to shape a person just as much as, or more than, the so-called big events.
Happenings that occurred when I was a child, needing to respond to the grown-up world, may have more to do with who sits before you than any philosophy or any knowledge.
Above all, my way seeking mind is a snapshot.
It is what I need to say today.
Five years ago or five years in the future, those would be very different way seeking mind talks.
Dogen wrote in Genjokoan 800 years ago:
*You see and understand only what your eye of practice can reach.
In order to learn the nature of the myriad things, you must know that although they may look round or square, the other features of oceans and mountains are infinite in variety.
Whole worlds are there.*
So this is my eye of practice, which can only see what I present, and only short clips of my life.
And then I also have opinions about what might have been important.
So I ask you to consider this talk as a heartfelt, sincere, but tentative and temporary expression.
And I ask for your understanding that the following is not a linear record of my practice or my life.
I grew up in Germany.
My father was an architect who lived for his work.
When I was small, he was in a partnership.
Later they split up and my dad ran his own office.
My mother was a housewife, [unclear: "was the mission to have"] her floors cleaner than most people's dishes.
I have one brother, whose name is Helmut, who is five years older than I am.
And he's the genius in the family.
In German style, he has a PhD in automotive engineering.
We were probably your standard dysfunctional family.
At times I think we were a bit ahead in the dysfunctionality department, but I could be wrong.
We were also not a very intimate family.
Our relationships were more run by: anything you say or do will be used against you.
Writing this way seeking mind talk was not that easy.
I could tell you about my past.
I could tell you about domestic violence.
I could say that when a human body falls against a wall, it makes a sound.
And it is terrible when you're a child and powerless.
You know that what your parents do to each other is wrong, but you cannot stop it or change it.
I could tell you that my dad was an alcoholic with serious Wednesday and Saturday morning hangovers and with the irrational temper of an alcoholic.
I could say that the appearance of a good family for outsiders was more important than having a functional and functioning family life.
I could tell you that my parents tried to shoehorn my brother into the norm.
He grew rebellious and then ended up in a boarding school.
I could tell you that I was sexually abused as a child.
I could tell you that for about a decade my dad didn't have time for family vacations, but that every year he had a week for his bowling buddies.
I could also tell you that my parents loved me very much.
They took great care of me.
They cleaned and fed me when I was a baby.
They worried about me through my childhood diseases, of which I had more than my share.
I had a good education.
I went through the German school system, with my dad especially making sure I was keeping up and that I was working hard.
And my dad was working so hard to provide for his family.
My mom kept a sparkling clean house and cooked three good meals every day.
She sewed some of my clothing when I was a child.
And the amazing thing is she never enjoyed the process.
She just worried about it and fussed about it, and it was only the product that counted.
But she still did it.
And she would knit wool hats for my brother and me.
I always had clean clothes.
At the boarding school my brother went to, for the first time he found a peer group that could actually outsmart him.
And all of a sudden he excelled and never stopped excelling.
He also holds several state, national, and international IPSC championships.
That's Practical Defense Shooting.
And to this day my parents love me very much.
They did the very best that they could do.
Both these stories are true.
The big question is: what am I?
Who am I?
Do I wish to define myself, or let these stories define me, and say I am this poor victim or I am this lucky person?
Which story am I?
Because stories are what we are.
Are the events I will recount truly what brought me here?
As soon as I write this down, as soon as I speak the words, it becomes a fixed story.
Please do not consider this as tentative.
But it's very tentative.
Here it goes.
The next one is interesting: my religious background.
First I would like to add my definition for religion, what the word means to me.
Yes, I do know that this definition is overly simplistic, but it's right out of my Kindle, so it has to be right.
And I hope that the rest of my talk is printed out here.
I'm getting blank pages.
*Religion is a belief in and worship of a superhuman controlling power, especially a personal god or gods.*
I am aware that there are many more definitions for religion, but I'm using this for now.
I grew up Roman Catholic.
I went to church as long as I had to.
Of course, as a very small child I really wanted to go, because it was the thing that the grownups did.
My parents had to drag me there as soon as the novelty wore off.
I left the church as soon as I had the willpower to take the fight with my parents all the way.
They were both practicing Catholics.
I felt I had numerous reasons: the way women were treated in and by the church.
I always said I would come back as soon as we have a female pope.
Original sin, especially original sin originating with women.
Fathers sacrificing their sons.
The claim that the church, as an uninvolved third party, could forgive wrongdoing, sins.
The story of Eve, the snake, and the fruit of knowledge.
That story always got to me.
I guess I've always been partial to snakes.
And let us not forget that the Friday pepperoni pizza did land you in hell, or at least increased your stint in purgatory.
At least that was the case until the mid-80s, when the roof just was tossed out, and now it's only Lent.
No meat in Lent on Fridays.
Oh, there are exceptions for that.

While traveling in South America, it's true, there was the persistent story that capybaras, capybara meat, could be eaten every day during Lent, since the world's largest rodent, which is a capybara, pig size, mostly lives in water.
It must be a fish.
My apologies for being flippant.
However, Catholicism simply did not take.
I stopped believing once I was old enough to have thoughts about it and to ask questions and not get answers.
In my search for words to explain my view after I gave up on Catholicism, I declared myself to be a humanist.

*Humanists endorse universal morality based on the commonality of human nature, and that knowledge of right and wrong is based on our best understanding of our individual and joint interests, rather than stemming from a transcendental or arbitrary local source, therefore rejecting faith as a basis for action.

The humanist ethics goal is a search for viable individual, social, and political principles of conduct, judging them on their ability to enhance human well-being, individual responsibility, ultimately trying to eliminate human suffering.*
I admit that I had never planned on a Zen practice.
I had zero interest in Buddhism, none.
In fact, for the first couple of years of my practice, I really tried to deny that Zen had much to do with Buddhism at all.
So how did I end up on this seat, giving this talk, being a priest?
Being shuso, by the way, is not a casual incidental happening.
There's a lot of intention behind it, I believe.
Well, it started with books.
I admit to loving The Tale of Genji.
In the 80s, I read [unclear: "The Thousand Shrine Warrior"] and The Little Zen Companion, and [unclear: "Bo Suzuki's DT and Junryu"] I read in the 90s.
I have a whole box, more than a decade's worth, of torn-off pages from the [unclear: "quoted-day"] Zen calendar.
I learned Zen like I tried to learn everything else: studying, reading.
Sooner or later, one stumbles across Zen koans.
So how about Mu?
The sound of one hand clapping, flags flapping, the price of rice, three pounds of flax, and trees falling in the forest.
Friends assured me that there was a response, but that this response was more a personal experience, and that telling me anything about it was not it.
What can I say?
That was not the answer I was looking for.
I was pretty sure at the time that if something was real and worthwhile, it could be communicated, explained, and put into words.
My next step was Thomas Cleary's translation of the Mumonkan.
For about five months, my first and last read of the day was reading a koan, holding it, and working with it in the way Thomas Cleary suggested in the preface to the book.
That was actually pretty cool.
My mind got a bit more quiet.
For the first time in my life, I wrote poetry.
Pretty good.
Nevertheless, I still felt there was something missing.
So I did what every serious spiritual seeker would do in my position.
I jumped on the computer and googled Bellingham and Zen.
Lo and behold, there was a Bellingham Zen practice group.
I got the contact information and called for an introductory session.
Jay did the intro before a Thursday sit, and there I thought I was on my way to figuring out those Zen koans.
I sat two periods of zazen.
Afterwards, I scrubbed the toilets.
It's kind of where I am right now.
And that was it.
I left, got into my car, started it, and the CD with my favorite song started to play.
It was Handsome Molly by Greg Brown.
It's still one of my favorite songs.
But for some reason, I reached over and turned it off.
Without thought, it just reached over.
So I must have liked that silence of the mind.
I kept on coming to zazen.
What else can I say?
It took me about three months to figure out there were two Zen sects, Soto and Rinzai.
And for the koan work I had envisioned, I had joined the wrong club.
Rinzai is what I wanted.
Soto is what I got.
But by the time I actually figured that out, I was hooked on this zazen way of life.
And I just couldn't really visualize myself sitting somewhere shouting [unclear: "moo"] during the night.
I continued to go to the Bellingham Zen practice group, which was our name at the time, to sit zazen.
I also admit that every once in a while, I would totally fall off the zazen wagon.
But then I would dust myself off and climb back on.
At times, I walked the path of anger.
At times, I walked the path of tears.
Most of the time, practice was changing me so slowly, I had no clue what was happening.
There were a few rare leaps of understanding, but my practice is mostly very, very, very boring.
Nothing happens, no grand experiences, no fireworks shooting off, no sparkles.
But my view of people and my view of actions must have changed, if I look back.
Oh, and I was still hung up on trying to find a teacher.
Remember, I was really wanting a Rinzai teacher, and I wanted to find my teacher.
I was not going to go with Norman, because he was everybody else's teacher, right?
I was going to find my very own teacher.
I know it was a really smart response to avoid Norman.
Just when he was around for talks or he came for retreat, I just didn't show up.
Avoidance really works, by the way.
Not.
I know that, but I finally encountered Norman during a hungry ghost ceremony at the old Dharma hall down the street.
And he addressed the hungry ghosts with such great attention, love, and care.
He spoke to them like you would address an old friend, with more attention than most people pay to the person they're speaking to.
He did not have a look at me, [unclear: "I'm a big teacher demeanor"] or attitude.
Within minutes, all my old reservations went out the window, and some months later, with a beating heart, I asked Norman to please accept me as his student.
And when he did, I was very happy.
Some years later, I was about to do Chukai, which is lay ordination, and to receive the lay precepts.
And the day before, I had [unclear: "Dokusama's"] Norman, and I told him I really, really could not do Chukai.
And he asked me why.
I had studied for it for a long time, I had waited for a long time, and I said I couldn't do it because I would probably burst into tears.
And remember what I said: my family just didn't do that, because it was used against you.
So I told him that it would be better if I just simply did not do it.
And he looked at me, and he said, "Chris, it actually would be really, really great if you could cry during Chukai."
He said there are many people who really don't cry easily, and if I cried, I would give them permission to cry with me.
He said, if there's anybody left who really cannot cry because they were hurt so badly, at some point I could cry for them.
So I did Chukai.
I did not cry.
I almost did, but not quite.
And for some strange reason, these words that Norman told me really stuck with me all these years.
My attitude changed.
My practice did cause significant changes, and I did have the great fortune to have Norman as my teacher.
His influence has changed my practice and my life and my work.
I remember telling Norman once that working with a sangha, of course, is different from working in real life.
I always wonder about this real life, and that deadlines and yeses and nos are much softer than they are between eight and five.
Norman said, "Well, that's true, Chris, but do you understand what your next challenge and intention should be?"
And I said, "No."
And this was his challenge.
He asked me to take my sangha work style to my eight to five job.
That is easier said than done if you work in code enforcement for a police department.
I should add that the Bellingham Police Department always was extremely supportive of my work and the way I was working.
So it was not as tough as I had made it in my mind.
I threw myself at evolving my work style.
When I started to work in enforcement in my late 20s, early 30s, I was looking at it as outwitting my opponent and, if necessary, cornering the adversary until there was no way out and I won.
Yeehaw.
Another victory for the righteous.
I was pretty effective and polite about it, so it wasn't totally horrid.
But my work really did evolve to the point that I saw enforcement work as an intricate dance between two partners who, by the way, greatly influence each other and each other's well-being.
To understand that my well-being was deeply informed by the care and attention and presence I offered the other person was quite a revelation.
In 2010, Norman ordained me.
My ordination name is Shudo Kanho, protector of the way, complete release.
I continue my practice and I continue my studies.
My love of the Dharma and the Sangha grows.
I was gone from Bellingham for about two years.
First I was doing some contract work in Santa Cruz, and then I spent three months of practice period at Tassajara Mountain Zen Center.
I want to thank all of you for the very warm welcome home.
To be back home, back with my home Sangha, to be allowed so generously to pick up my practice again among you, almost like I was never gone, is overwhelmingly beautiful at times.
I am very grateful for this.
Also your tolerance of me being a Dharma geek at times, and the great discussions we have.
It's good to be back in my work life, in my conventional life.
I was always working towards goals, mostly with performance benchmarks and personal timelines.
I strive to achieve my targets by this deadline, and so on.
Fortunately, slowly but surely I have been dropping this goal-driven thinking out of my life and most definitely out of my Zen practice.
I am going one step at a time.
Oh, I made another discovery.
I found that all my well-laid plans do not work out, not a single time ever.
Little particles of it here and there come through, but the big picture that I paint in my mind doesn't happen.
Not ever, never ever.
Because I make all these plans, and in the meantime real life is happening, and this real life does not care one bit about my plans.
Reality happens.
Things I could never ever imagine appear.
So now I try to go one step at a time.
I try not to have too many opinions about what things should look like.
It would be way more boring if things actually would happen the way I envision them.
Life would be so limited if it were limited to my imagination and my plans.
So I do not know where I will end up and what the view will be like when I get there.
And that is okay.
There is a quote I really, really like.
It's out of the book I Am That by Sri Nisargadatta Maharaj, and it goes like this:
*Love says I am everything.
Wisdom says I am nothing.
And between the two my life flows.*
Thank you very much for your patience with this way seeking mind talk.
I was wondering if anybody had any questions or comments, because I did promise I would string it out a little bit more.
Okay.
Yes, Nancy.
**Participant:** Casually, I said something in my usual form of styling.
I said, you know, and the answer is, since I have been practicing I really have discovered that people are just thinking about themselves.
They're not really worried about whether you're perfect or not.
You show up on time.
Well, wait a minute.
Take that back, and show up on time.
But I was thinking about that a lot last night, because I think of Zen as somehow everybody caring about one another.
But the other part of me, especially the therapist part of me, agrees.
We are all concerned mostly with ourselves, even in our actions.
